D010_l001.question:
A 33-year-old single female who works as a freelance writer presents with a one-month history of elevated mood with irritable features, during which she exhibited persistent psychomotor agitation, characterized by an inability to remain still and a constant need to engage in activity. She displayed pressured speech, speaking rapidly and nonstop, with a subjective sense of mental acceleration and an inability to control or slow down her thoughts. Attention was markedly impaired, with frequent distractibility and an inability to sustain focus on tasks. Concurrent with this period, she experienced gustatory hallucinations, reporting bitter and metallic tastes in the absence of any physiological cause. These psychotic symptoms were temporally limited to the period of mood elevation and did not persist beyond it.

This manic episode was preceded by a four-month depressive episode marked by loss of interest in usual activities, early insomnia, and psychomotor retardation, evidenced by slowed speech and prolonged response latency. She endorsed pervasive loss of energy, significant unintentional weight loss exceeding 5% of body mass, and delusional guilt, expressing fixed beliefs that she was responsible for unrelated adverse events. Additionally, she reported recurrent, intrusive suicidal impulses involving urges to jump from heights or step into traffic, though without specific planning or intent. Both mood episodes resulted in marked functional impairment.
D010_l001.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D010_l001.answer: A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D010_l002.question:
A 56-year-old divorced male who works as a lawyer presents with a one-month duration of elevated mood characterized by persistent euphoria, increased vitality, and unwarranted optimism. During this period, he exhibited psychomotor agitation, relentless talkativeness, and racing thoughts with frequent shifts in topic. His attention was markedly distractible, consistently drawn to ambient environmental stimuli such as distant sounds and peripheral movements. Concomitantly, he experienced visual hallucinations involving the perception of individuals not present. These psychotic features emerged during the mood disturbance and resolved as the episode remitted. There was significant functional impairment, including disrupted work performance and strained interpersonal interactions.

This manic episode was preceded by a four-month episode of depression marked by persistent loss of energy, psychomotor retardation, diminished appetite, and non-restorative sleep. He displayed marked indifference to professional accomplishments, recurrent feelings of worthlessness, and intermittent suicidal ideation involving impulses to jump from elevated places, though without intent or plan. No psychotic features were reported during this depressive period. The depressive episode also resulted in substantial functional decline. Mood symptoms are not attributable to substance use or another medical condition.
D010_l002.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D010_l002.answer: A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D010_l003.question:
A 33-year-old female, single and working as a freelance writer, presents with a one-month history of manic symptoms and a preceding four-month depressive episode, both associated with significant functional impairment. During the manic phase, the patient exhibited marked mood lability with cycling between euphoria and irritability, psychomotor agitation, and pressured speech characterized by an inability to remain silent and a rapid, unrelenting flow of verbal output. She reported a subjective inability to control or slow racing thoughts and demonstrated marked distractibility, with an inability to sustain attention across tasks. Concurrent with the manic episode, she experienced tactile hallucinations involving the sensation of being touched in the absence of external stimuli. These psychotic features were present only during the period of elevated mood and did not persist into mood-stable or depressive states.

The preceding depressive episode was characterized by anhedonia, initial insomnia, psychomotor retardation of speech with prolonged latency in responding, loss of energy, and notable weight gain exceeding 5% of body weight within one month. She developed delusional guilt, believing herself responsible for unrelated adverse events despite lack of evidence. This episode included a prior suicide attempt with preparatory behaviors. There is no indication that the psychotic symptoms occurred outside the context of the manic episode.
D010_l003.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D010_l003.answer: A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D010_l004.question:
A 22-year-old single female who works as a pet groomer presented with a one-month episode of elevated mood lability, characterized by abrupt shifts between euphoria and irritability, accompanied by markedly increased psychomotor activity and subjective energy. During this period, she exhibited pressured speech that was rapid and difficult to interrupt, with frequent derailment in thought process secondary to marked distractibility from extraneous environmental stimuli. She reported persistent racing thoughts that she was unable to regulate or suppress. Concurrent with this episode, she experienced tactile hallucinations, describing the sensation of insects crawling on her skin in the absence of any identifiable stimulus. These psychotic symptoms were only present during the period of mood elevation and increased energy.

This manic episode followed a four-month depressive episode marked by persistent low mood, psychomotor slowing with delayed verbal responsiveness, and profound physical fatigue. She demonstrated significant social withdrawal, markedly reduced appetite, and a greater than 5% reduction in body weight over one month. Sleep was disrupted by recurrent, vivid nightmares. She endorsed delusional beliefs regarding personal responsibility for unrelated adverse events and reported passive death ideation, though without suicidal intent.

The manic and depressive episodes were each associated with clinically significant functional impairment. The psychotic features resolved outside the context of mood elevation.

A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D010_l004.answer: A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D010_l005.question:

D010_l006.question:

Thought processes were disorganized, with reported racing thoughts and frequent derailment. A notable increase in goal-directed activity was accompanied by decreased need for sleep and hypersexual behavior, including inappropriate advances toward colleagues.

During the same episode, the patient developed psychotic symptoms, including complex visual hallucinations involving perceived figures in her environment and referential delusions, in which she interpreted neutral events and ambient conversations as having personal and symbolic meaning directed at her. These psychotic features occurred exclusively during the period of mood elevation and increased energy. There is no evidence of independent psychotic episodes outside affective disturbance.

The episode has resulted in marked functional impairment, including difficulties maintaining occupational responsibilities and interpersonal relationships. There is no history of major depressive episodes reported during this period.

A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)

D010_l007.question:

D010_l009.question:

She reported racing thoughts that shifted rapidly between unrelated concepts, impairing coherent focus. She also reported episodic tactile hallucinations, describing sensations of being touched or brushed on the skin without external stimuli.

    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)

D010_l010.question:
A healthy 18-year-old male, single and currently a high school senior, presents for psychiatric evaluation following a two-month period of marked behavioral and mood disturbance. Over this duration, the patient exhibited a distinct episode of elevated and labile mood, fluctuating between euphoria and irritability, accompanied by psychomotor agitation, pressured speech, and an unrelenting stream of racing thoughts that he describes as uncontrollable. The patient reports significantly increased goal-directed activity, manifesting as engagement in multiple academic and extracurricular projects simultaneously, far exceeding his prior level of involvement. This pattern of behavior has led to substantial functional impairment, interfering with his academic performance and interpersonal relationships.

Concurrent with the onset of mood elevation, the patient developed psychotic symptoms, including complex auditory hallucinations consisting of multiple voices commenting on his actions in the absence of external stimuli. Additionally, he endorsed nihilistic delusions, expressing a fixed belief that societal collapse is imminent and unavoidable. These psychotic features emerged during the mood episode and are not present outside of this clinical context. There is no history of substance use or medical illness that accounts for the symptom profile. The course of illness is consistent with a single, continuous manic episode with mood-incongruent psychotic features.

A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Bipolar I Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)

D010_l011.question:

He reported pervasive feelings of worthlessness and expressed indifference toward professional accomplishments that had once been central to his identity. These psychotic features occurred exclusively during the period of mood elevation and resolved as the episode abated. 

The episode was associated with marked functional impairment, resulting in academic probation and social conflict. No history of depressive or mixed episodes was reported during this period.

D010_l025.question:
A 58-year-old male, married and working as a Building Maintenance Supervisor, presents with a 3-month-long episode of markedly elevated psychomotor activity and severe mood disturbance. He reports a significant increase in energy, describing himself as “wired” and requiring only 2–3 hours of sleep per night without fatigue. Speech is markedly pressured, with rapid, loud, and continuous verbal output that interrupts conversational flow and prevents dialogue. Sustained attention is impaired, with frequent shifting between incomplete tasks and an inability to follow through on directed activities.  

The patient has initiated multiple new work projects beyond his job scope, often directing staff without authorization, reflecting occupational hyperactivity. Concurrently, he has engaged in extensive, impulsive spending sprees, including large purchases of unnecessary equipment and electronics, resulting in notable financial strain.  

Delusional content is present, including grandiose beliefs of having a divine mandate to “rebuild civilization” and erotomanic convictions that a public figure is sending him encrypted messages of romantic affection. No hallucinations are reported outside the context of this episode.  

All psychotic features emerged contemporaneously with the onset of mood and behavioral symptoms and have persisted throughout the episode. There is clear evidence of severe functional impairment in occupational and interpersonal domains. Psychotic symptoms are confined to the period of mood elevation and increased energy.

    B. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)

    D. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
